# Teaching and review

**Professional graphics and embedded navigation (John, 2026-09-30, MIT Lectures journal 0009).** Mathematical graphics must be clean and easy to follow: readable labels, a clear focal operation, faithful geometry, and no overlaps or unearned decorative complexity. Verify the actual artifact through its normal reading surface, including every embedded local document/source link and working visual control, not only the top-level register link. A query-based viewer may not resolve relative assets or links; use its supported document route or self-contained delivery. Treat a reported quality failure separately from any transport defect; a repaired stylesheet alone does not establish that the graphics now meet the learner's expectations.

**Intent fit before a rebuild (John, 2026-09-30, MIT Lectures journal 0007).** A numerically correct worked example does not establish that the learner's actual question was answered. For an architecture explanation, keep the requested block diagram as the reference and show each block's input, operation, output and purpose, including where its starting representations and learned parameters come from. Test the learner's stated hypotheses explicitly. Distinguish illustrative vector geometry from measured trained-model behavior. When John requests a plan and mockups before production, discover unresolved design choices one at a time and show those artifacts before rebuilding the pack. Mathematics and agent-review passes must not be presented as evidence of learner satisfaction.

Beginner default: assume familiarity with everyday arithmetic and reading a picture, not with the subject's terminology. Even notation such as membership, inequalities, braces and indices needs a first concrete use. A prerequisite refresher should resolve the immediate question and return promptly to the main thread.

Every visual has a question, prediction, visible change, interpretation and limitation. A finite illustration does not prove an infinite assertion; sampled behavior does not establish a universal law. Keep represented objects fixed when a control merely reclassifies them. Use labels or patterns as well as color. A flashcard reveal should highlight the relevant distinction, not repeat the same picture beside more prose.

John's first Math541 feedback adds a concrete acceptance check: the reader must know why the concept matters, state its rigorous definition, recognize both a working case and a failing case, identify exactly why it fails, and see the consequence for a meaningful task. Put those cases in the core explanation. Keep the formal definition distinct from its plain-language interpretation; short takeaway bullets make the structure recoverable. A downstream application preview must state its assumptions and be labelled as a preview if its prerequisites are taught later.

For cover graphics, draw actual interval bands and target points/intervals on the same scale with vertical alignment. Tell the reader which row is the target and which rows are supplied members. Explicitly distinguish a collection that fails to cover at all, a cover whose chosen finite selection fails, and a cover for which every finite selection fails. Show the missed point. Multiple-choice cards should use readable answer text, explain wrong alternatives and let the learner retry without presenting a guessed answer as understanding.

Every worked solution includes the full problem, what makes it difficult, the needed concept, strategy, justified steps, a result check and a transferable takeaway. Use ordinary language beside formulas. Teach one clear method before adding alternatives. Increasing difficulty should come from a new combination of learned ideas, not unexplained machinery.

For real-line analysis: state the ambient space; distinguish element versus subset, sequence versus range set versus series, approaching a point versus containing it, point-dependent radius versus a uniform radius, and one cover versus every cover. A subcover selects original members. Finite need not mean minimal. Closed-and-bounded characterizes compactness in Euclidean space, not in every metric space.

For statistics: distinguish population, one observed sample, an estimator and its sampling distribution. Every number and figure must come from the same declared data/model. Show the computation before interpreting it. A realistic case needs a credible decision and mechanism.

Adversarial review asks: where would a novice get stuck; what tempting wrong conclusion does this display suggest; which hypothesis is essential; which unfamiliar problem demonstrates transfer; where do hints become an answer key; can the student open and operate this without knowing our implementation? Keep source accuracy, mathematical correctness, teaching quality and rendered delivery as separate evidence. Agent review does not establish measured learning gains.

Apply the Foundry Elegance Law to the process AND the material. Keep necessary foundations, complete explanation and useful software. Cut decorative interactions, duplicate documents, unrelated detours and review rituals without new findings. The student's effort is part of the cost being minimized.

Motivation acceptance: the learner can follow each visual change and explain why it changes the conclusion before reading the formula. Separate a ceiling from an attained result; generic pictures must not hide the decisive missing point. Named theorem links open a local statement plus intuition and example. Label external sources as optional reading and link to the relevant section.

Problem-to-memory acceptance: each problem names the concepts actually needed by its checked solution; the lesson teaches them, the cards drill their definitions and reasoning, and each hint corresponds to an identified solution step. No hint is authored from the problem statement alone. Test unaided recall with choices hidden and no stale revealed answer. Generate identical problem IDs/statements in the problems-only, hints and separately released solution views. Require full justified reasoning and purposeful graphics in the solutions, not answer keys alone.

Recall-front audit: inspect rendered text, endpoint labels, captions and accessible descriptions, not just the hidden choices. A question asking the learner to compute interval endpoints must not print those computed endpoints on its front. Show the givens and reserve the computed result for reveal. Interpretive diagrams may show the given objects; distinguish those from the requested answer.
